VBO:0200070.summary: Curious, sociable and energetic, the Ardennes Cattle Dog can be obstinate and courageous when defending its people or territory. Belgian drovers shaped it for the hard work of gathering, driving and guarding cattle in rough Ardennes terrain and weather. Nineteenth-century herds could include sheep, pigs and horses alongside the dairy cattle.
VBO:0200070.shortDescription: Curious and courageous, this Belgian drover worked cattle through the rough Ardennes hills.
VBO:0200070.historicalRoots: Belgian Ardennes cattle drover and guard dog shaped by severe weather and difficult terrain.

sources.title: FCI: Bouvier des Ardennes (Standard No. 171)
sources.evidence: FCI identifies Ardennes cattle droving and guarding, hard terrain and climate, energetic playful curious sociable temperament, tenacity and defensive courage; many naturally short-tailed dogs and harsh weatherproof coat.

VBO:0200117.summary: Lively and courageous, the Bosnian Barak follows scent persistently and gives a ringing voice that can carry high or deep across a trail. The FCI first registered this robust hound as the Illyrian Hound in 1965; its later Bosnian Broken-Haired Hound name reflects its origin and rough coat.
VBO:0200117.shortDescription: Lively and persistent, the shaggy Bosnian Barak follows a scent trail with a ringing voice.
VBO:0200117.historicalRoots: Bosnian broken-haired scent hound, formerly registered by FCI as the Illyrian Hound.

sources.title: FCI: Bosnian Broken-Haired Hound – Barak (Standard No. 155)
sources.evidence: FCI describes lively, courageous, persistent scent-hound temperament, sonorous voice, long shaggy coat, bushy eyebrows, earthy gray or reddish-yellow color and renaming from Illyrian Hound.

VBO:0200166.summary: Intelligent and courageous, Billy hounds bring remarkable speed to traditional pack hunting. Developed in western-central France in the nineteenth century from older, now-extinct hound lines, they still pursue roe deer and wild boar in packs.
VBO:0200166.shortDescription: Fast and courageous, the pale French Billy hunts roe deer and wild boar with a pack.
VBO:0200166.historicalRoots: Nineteenth-century western-central French pack hound used for roe deer and wild boar.

sources.title: FCI: Billy (Standard No. 25)
sources.evidence: FCI confirms French large scent hound; strong yet light form, fine head, long tail, short harsh pale white to light orange/lemon coat. UKC breed standard supplies nineteenth-century western-central French origin, roe deer and wild-boar pack use, intelligence, courage and speed.

sources.title: United Kennel Club: Billy Breed Standard
sources.evidence: UKC documents nineteenth-century western-central France, roe deer/wild boar pack hunting, intelligence, courage and speed.

VBO:0200188.summary: Devoted and readily trained, the Bohemian Wire-Haired Pointing Griffon works across field, water and woodland. Known as the Český fousek, it was the region’s most widely kept wirehaired pointer before World War I. After the breed nearly disappeared in the 1920s, planned breeding from surviving typical dogs restored it.
VBO:0200188.shortDescription: Devoted and versatile, this bearded Czech pointer works field, water and woodland.
VBO:0200188.historicalRoots: Czech wire-haired multipurpose pointer restored after severe post-World War I decline.

sources.title: FCI: Český Fousek (Standard No. 245)
sources.evidence: FCI details field/water/woodland versatility, devotion and trainability, near-extinction after World War I and restoration from typical survivors; medium-large wire-haired pointer with distinctive brows and beard.

VBO:0200226.summary: Braques Français of the Pyrenean type are gentle and close to their people, yet quick and spirited when searching a field. They tend to maintain a steady gallop, while the larger Gascogne type alternates trotting and galloping. Both descend from French pointing dogs long valued for a methodical search and responsiveness to training.
VBO:0200226.shortDescription: Gentle with people yet spirited afield, this lighter French pointer moves with a steady gallop.
VBO:0200226.historicalRoots: Smaller, lighter Pyrenean type of the Braque Français pointing tradition.

sources.title: FCI: Braque Français, Pyrenean Type (Standard No. 134)
sources.evidence: FCI distinguishes the smaller lighter Pyrenean from the Gascogne type, short coat, pointer utility and allowed natural short tail. Société Centrale Canine breed-club commentary describes gentle close-to-people temperament and quicker, more constant gallop than Gascogne.

sources.title: Société Centrale Canine: Braque Français Standard Commenté
sources.evidence: Official French breed commentary describes temperament outside the hunt and distinguishes quicker, constant Pyrenean gallop from Gascogne.

VBO:0200437.summary: Calm and good-natured, Deutsch Langhaars work across field, forest and water, before and after a shot. Their ancestry combines dogs used for birds, falconry and water work with German scent hounds. Breeders began keeping the line pure in 1879, and Baron von Schorlemer wrote its first standard in 1897.
VBO:0200437.shortDescription: Calm and good-natured, this long-haired German pointer works field, forest and water.
VBO:0200437.historicalRoots: German versatile long-haired pointing dog, with documented pure breeding from 1879.

sources.title: FCI: German Long-Haired Pointing Dog (Standard No. 117)
sources.evidence: FCI records balanced calm good-natured temperament, versatile field/water/forest work, bird/hawk/water-dog/scent-hound origins and pure breeding since 1879; feathered coat and horizontal tail.

VBO:0200440.summary: Deutscher Wachtelhunds are lively, friendly and assured, selected to flush game from cover and track wounded quarry. The breed works independently while keeping contact with a handler, using voice and nose in woods and water. Its German stud-book history began around the turn of the twentieth century, with brown and roan strains maintained as distinct color lines.
VBO:0200440.shortDescription: Lively and assured, this German flushing dog uses nose and voice in woodland cover and water.
VBO:0200440.historicalRoots: German flushing and tracking dog with stud-book breeding from around 1900.

sources.title: FCI: Deutscher Wachtelhund (Standard No. 104)
sources.evidence: FCI details lively friendly assured temperament, independent flushing, tracking wounded game, nose/voice, woods and water work, early stud book and brown/roan color lines.

VBO:0200567.summary: German Hounds follow scent with a clear voice, an old Bracke trait prized during their long hare-hunting history. Around 1900, breeders joined the Sauerländer Holzbracke with local Steinbracken to establish the Deutsche Bracke. The breed now also works driven hunts, where its reliable trail voice remains valued.
VBO:0200567.shortDescription: Vocal on a scent trail, the tricolor Deutsche Bracke carries an old German hare-hunting tradition.
VBO:0200567.historicalRoots: German Deutsche Bracke formed by Westphalian and local Steinbracke lines around 1900.

sources.title: FCI: German Hound / Deutsche Bracke (Standard No. 299)
sources.evidence: FCI details Westphalian Holzbracke and local Steinbracke consolidation around 1900, light high-legged conformation, tricolor and thick tail. German Hunting Association primary brochure describes reliably vocal trail work, historical hare specialization and modern driven hunts.

sources.title: Deutscher Jagdverband: Jagdhunde, Deutsche Bracke profile
sources.evidence: German Hunting Association documents spur-/fährtenlaut trail work, historical hare hunting and present driven-hunt use.

VBO:0200575.summary: German Roughhaired Pointers are calm, self-controlled and courageous gundogs that remain tractable while working. Also called Deutsch Stichelhaar, the breed descends from an old rough-coated German partridge-dog line rather than the German Shorthaired Pointer. In 1888, Hans von Kadisch established that separate lineage; breeders later rebuilt the type from a small surviving population.
VBO:0200575.shortDescription: Calm and self-controlled, the Deutsch Stichelhaar follows an old German pointing line distinct from the shorthaired pointer.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 232: German Roughhaired Pointer
sources.evidence: FCI 232 states versatile tractable working gundog; balanced, calm, courageous, self-controlled temperament; old rough-coated German partridge-dog lineage distinct from Shorthaired Pointer.

VBO:0200660.summary: Harriers are outgoing, friendly scenthounds bred to pursue hares in a pack. English hunters followed them on horseback or on foot as the ground allowed, while the dogs held to a hare's looping scent trail. That task called for maneuverability and persistence when the trail doubled back across rough country.
VBO:0200660.shortDescription: An outgoing English pack hound, the Harrier follows a hare’s twisting scent trail with speed and persistence.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 295: Harrier
sources.evidence: FCI 295 establishes medium scenthound, lighter than Foxhound and sure gait; AKC Harrier breed information describes outgoing, friendly pack hound bred to chase hare; AKC history explains pace and tracking persistence.

sources.title: American Kennel Club: Harrier
sources.evidence: Outgoing, friendly, prey-driven English pack hound developed to pursue hare.

sources.title: American Kennel Club: Harrier history
sources.evidence: English pack hunting; pace suitable to horse riders and scent persistence on twisting hare trail.

VBO:0200832.summary: Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdogs are lively, resourceful herders with a habit of taking initiative. Their attachment to the shepherd comes with a headstrong streak and caution toward strangers. They developed in the French Pyrenees, where small, quick dogs worked across mountain pastures.
VBO:0200832.shortDescription: Quick and resourceful on mountain pasture, this Pyrenean herder takes initiative and bonds closely with its shepherd.
VBO:0200832.historicalRoots: Pyrenean mountain herding dog, long-haired variety
editorialFamilies: Pyrenean mountain herding dog, long-haired variety

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 141: Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI 141 identifies long-haired Pyrenean Sheepdog, courageous/resourceful initiative, devotion to shepherd, headstrong and wary-stranger character, French Pyrenean pastoral roots.

VBO:0200211.summary: Brindle Boxers are typically self-assured and watchful, with a cheerful, playful side around familiar people. Their willingness to work with a handler helps explain the breed’s use as a companion and guard. The Brabant Bullenbeisser, an ancestor of the Boxer, once held quarry until hunters arrived.
VBO:0200211.shortDescription: Playful with familiar people and watchful around strangers, the brindle Boxer is keen to work with a handler.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 144: Boxer
sources.evidence: FCI 144 describes Boxer as self-confident, calm/equable, friendly in play, watchful and loyal to household; Brabant Bullenbeisser ancestry; explicitly defines the brindle variety as contrasting dark stripes over fawn ground and normal-length natural tail.

VBO:0200997.summary: Perdiguero de Burgos dogs are calm, docile hunters with a strong nose and a firm, persistent way of following a trail. The Spanish pointer is valued for pointing and retrieving feathered and small game across difficult ground. Though usually trained for smaller quarry, the breed also has a history of boldly tackling larger game.
VBO:0200997.shortDescription: Calm and persistent, this Burgos pointer uses a keen nose to track, point and retrieve across rough ground.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 90: Perdiguero de Burgos
sources.evidence: FCI 90 describes calm, docile, obedient temperament, excellent nose, firm tracking, pointing and retrieving on difficult terrain.

VBO:0201155.summary: Russian-European Laikas are steady, even-tempered hunting dogs with a keen nose for detecting game. They come from the forest regions of European Russia, where regional Laika populations were brought under a single breed name in 1947. The purebred standard was approved in 1952, after a longer process of selective breeding.
VBO:0201155.shortDescription: Even-tempered and keen-nosed, this Russian forest hunter was consolidated from regional Laika lines after World War II.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 304: Russian-European Laika
sources.evidence: FCI 304 describes steady/even temperament, developed scent and game-finding work, European Russian forest origin, regional Laika consolidation and 1952 standard.

VBO:0201167.summary: Saint Miguel Cattle Dogs are determined drovers and attentive guardians from São Miguel in the Azores, receptive to their owners yet wary of strangers. When driving dairy cattle, they have a distinctive working habit: nipping low to avoid injuring the udder.
VBO:0201167.shortDescription: An Azorean cattle drover, this determined dog works carefully with dairy herds and stays responsive to its owner.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 340: Saint Miguel Cattle Dog
sources.evidence: FCI 340 identifies São Miguel/Azores origin, cattle driving and guarding, determined toward strangers, docile/receptive with owner, low nipping to spare dairy udders.

VBO:0200716.summary: Italian Rough-Haired Segugi are poised, reserved hounds that pursue scent with drive and endurance. Generally calmer and less exuberant than the smooth-coated Segugio, they hunt alone or in a pack across difficult mountain ground. A resonant voice carries through their pursuit of hare and wild boar.
VBO:0200716.shortDescription: Poised and more reserved than its smooth-coated cousin, this Italian hound follows hard trails with a resonant voice.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 198: Italian Rough-Haired Segugio
sources.evidence: FCI 198 says rough-haired Segugio is reserved, calm and poised versus smooth variety; works ardently alone or pack on difficult terrain; resonant voice; hare and boar use.

VBO:0200719.summary: Steady but not especially outgoing, the Italian Short-Haired Segugio becomes eager and persistent on a scent. Alone or with a pack, this hound follows hare and wild boar across varied terrain with speed, endurance and a resonant voice.
VBO:0200719.shortDescription: Steady and reserved away from work, this smooth-coated Italian hound grows eager on a scent trail.
VBO:0200719.historicalRoots: Italian scent hound with a distinct short-haired FCI standard; traditionally used especially for hare and wild boar.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 337 — Italian Short-Haired Segugio
sources.evidence: Temperament describes a steady, less outgoing but extremely eager hound with a resonant voice; utilization and behavior cover hare and wild boar, varied terrain, and solo or pack work. The standard explicitly defines the short coat.

VBO:0200310.summary: Affectionate and friendly, the black-and-tan Cavalier King Charles Spaniel shares the breed's cheerful, sporting confidence. Cavaliers were treasured as companion spaniels while sturdier forebears also went afield; British breeders restored the longer-muzzled type in the 1920s after Roswell Eldridge's Crufts challenge.
VBO:0200310.shortDescription: Affectionate and spirited, this black-and-tan Cavalier shares the breed's companion and sporting roots.
VBO:0200310.historicalRoots: British toy spaniel revived as a distinct longer-muzzled Cavalier type in the 1920s; black and tan is one of four FCI colors.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 136 — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
sources.evidence: One sporting, affectionate, fearless, friendly temperament applies to every color; black and tan is explicitly recognized with raven black and bright tan markings.

sources.title: AKC — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel History
sources.evidence: Historical account describes toy companion and bird-hunting spaniels, Eldridge's 1926 Crufts challenge, and the breed club formed in 1928 to restore the older longer-muzzled type.

VBO:0200311.summary: Sporting and affectionate, the Blenheim Cavalier brings a lively spaniel spirit to a companion breed. Red-and-white spaniels at the Duke of Marlborough's Blenheim estate were kept for both company and bird hunting; their name survives in this color. The modern Cavalier was revived in Britain in the 1920s around the older, longer-muzzled type.
VBO:0200311.shortDescription: Affectionate and sporting, the Blenheim Cavalier carries a companion-and-bird-hunting history.
VBO:0200311.historicalRoots: The Blenheim color recalls the Duke of Marlborough's red-and-white spaniels; the modern British Cavalier type was revived in the 1920s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 136 — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
sources.evidence: Shared sporting, affectionate, fearless, friendly character and the precise Blenheim rich-chestnut-on-white variety are defined by the standard.

sources.title: AKC — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel History
sources.evidence: Documents the Blenheim estate's red-and-white spaniels as lap companions and bird hunters, and the 1920s revival of the older longer-muzzled type.

VBO:0200312.summary: Friendly, affectionate and often ready for activity, the ruby Cavalier shares the sporting temperament of the other Cavalier colors. The breed's British revival grew from a 1926 challenge to recover the longer-faced spaniels seen in portraits from Charles II's time; its older toy-spaniel lineage combined close companionship with an outdoor streak.
VBO:0200312.shortDescription: Friendly and affectionate, the ruby Cavalier shares the breed's lively sporting and companion history.
VBO:0200312.historicalRoots: British toy spaniel revived in the 1920s from older longer-faced spaniel ideals; ruby is the FCI's solid-red color variety.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 136 — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
sources.evidence: Describes a sporting, affectionate, fearless and friendly breed; ruby is specified as the whole-colored rich-red variety without white markings.

sources.title: AKC — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel History
sources.evidence: Documents toy-spaniel companionship, occasional bird hunting by sturdier predecessors, and the 1926 Eldridge challenge that led to revival of the older type.

VBO:0200313.summary: Cheerful and affectionate, the tricolour Cavalier has the same confident sporting character as its fellow color varieties. Its toy-spaniel forebears were companions in Britain, while some still went out to flush birds; a 1920s breed revival sought the longer-faced spaniels depicted in earlier royal-era art.
VBO:0200313.shortDescription: Cheerful and affectionate, the tricolour Cavalier has the breed's sporting spark and companion roots.
VBO:0200313.historicalRoots: British companion spaniel with bird-hunting predecessors; revived as the longer-faced Cavalier type in the 1920s, with tricolour among four FCI varieties.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 136 — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
sources.evidence: Shared sporting, affectionate, fearless, friendly temperament and tricolour's black, white and tan distribution are specified.

sources.title: AKC — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel History
sources.evidence: Documents royal-era toy-spaniel companionship, bird-flushing work by some predecessors, and the 1920s restoration of the older longer-muzzled type.

VBO:0200443.summary: Calm and devoted to familiar people, the black-and-rust Dobermann is alert, confident and keen to work. Friedrich Louis Dobermann developed the breed in 1870s Germany from protective working dogs. It went on to serve as a guard and police dog, earning the nickname 'Gendarme dog.'
VBO:0200443.shortDescription: Calm and devoted, this black-and-rust Dobermann carries an alert working character and police history.
VBO:0200443.historicalRoots: German working breed developed by Friedrich Louis Dobermann in the 1870s; later used as a guard and police dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 143 — Dobermann
sources.evidence: History names Friedrich Louis Dobermann, 1870s origin and police work; temperament calls for calm devotion, alertness and willingness to work, shared by black and brown varieties; color section defines rust-red markings.

VBO:0200444.summary: Friendly and steady with familiar people, the brown-and-rust Dobermann shares the breed's self-confident, attentive working character. Friedrich Louis Dobermann built this German line from protective working dogs in the 1870s. Later guard and police work made the breed known as the 'Gendarme dog.'
VBO:0200444.shortDescription: Friendly, steady and attentive, this brown-and-rust Dobermann shares the breed's German working roots.
VBO:0200444.historicalRoots: German breed shaped in the 1870s for protective work and later police service; brown with rust-red markings is an FCI-recognized variety.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 143 — Dobermann
sources.evidence: Standard describes friendly, calm, devoted, attentive, confident working temperament and history from Friedrich Louis Dobermann to guard and police service; brown with clean rust-red markings is one of two coat colors.

VBO:0200897.summary: Alert and fearless, the black-and-silver Miniature Schnauzer carries a watchful, tenacious character. German farmers developed these small dogs to pursue rodents in houses and barns; the color now called black and silver was once described as black and tan. The breed also settled into a companion and watchdog role.
VBO:0200897.shortDescription: Alert and fearless, this black-and-silver Miniature Schnauzer carries a German farm-ratting past.
VBO:0200897.historicalRoots: Developed in Germany around the turn of the twentieth century; black-and-silver descended from an earlier black-and-tan color designation.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 183 — Miniature Schnauzer
sources.evidence: Temperament describes alertness, fearlessness and endurance; history traces the breed to Frankfurt/Main; black-and-silver coat requirements are explicit.

sources.title: AKC — Miniature Schnauzer History
sources.evidence: Describes German farm development for indoor/barn rodent control and records how the older black-and-tan designation became black and silver.

VBO:0200898.summary: Fearless and watchful, the pepper-and-salt Miniature Schnauzer brings a durable little dog's energy to its companion role. The breed emerged around Frankfurt from smaller rough-haired farm dogs, then earned its place as a sharp-eyed household watchdog; German farmers also bred Minis to pursue rats and other small pests indoors and around barns.
VBO:0200898.shortDescription: Fearless and watchful, this pepper-and-salt Miniature Schnauzer recalls the breed's farm-ratting roots.
VBO:0200898.historicalRoots: German breed shaped near Frankfurt around 1900 from smaller rough-haired dogs; pepper-and-salt is an FCI-recognized coat variety.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 183 — Miniature Schnauzer
sources.evidence: History places the breed near Frankfurt and describes its rough-coated development; temperament supports fearlessness, endurance and alert household watchfulness; pepper and salt is defined in color section.

sources.title: AKC — Miniature Schnauzer History
sources.evidence: Documents German farmers developing small Schnauzers for rodent control in the house and barn.
